essay:
# A reading both sides predicted settles nothing.

Two forecasters can watch the same number climb and both be right, because each of them predicted it. Most arguments about where AI goes next are like that: the evidence each side points to fits the other side's story too. For each question the outlook turns on, this page sets out what named writers argue, what each side expects this site's readings to show, what they show tonight, and the reading that would tell the sides apart.

### Folio I · Can AI do whole jobs, reliably?

## Fast progress on single skills is what both sides expect; whole jobs are the test

The fastest story starts with a loop. Daniel Kokotajlo, who worked on governance at OpenAI, and his fellow forecasters at the AI Futures Project wrote AI 2027, a dated story in which each AI model, a program trained on text and data to write and reason, helps build the next, so progress feeds on itself until AI outdoes people at almost everything by the end of 2027 [cite:ai_2027]. They called 2027 their single most likely year rather than their middle estimate. They pushed their dates later at the end of 2025 and moved them earlier again in 2026, because coding agents, models set to carry out tasks on their own, improved faster than they had expected [cite:ai_futures_update]; their own check finds events running a little slower than the story [cite:ai_futures_q25].

Benjamin Jones, an economist at Northwestern who studies where growth and discoveries come from, answers with arithmetic. Research is a chain of steps and needs every one of them, so making some steps superhumanly fast leaves the rest, still slow, to set the pace, as a line of walkers moves at the speed of its slowest member. In his words, "bottlenecks severely mute the effect of extremely productive AI" [cite:jones_b]. What counts is the share of steps AI can take over.

Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Arvind Narayanan and their colleagues, computer scientists at Princeton who test AI agents, add that getting a task right is not getting it right every time: agents that solve more tasks each year still give different answers when the same task is run again, and a firm hands over work only when the answer is dependable [cite:agent_reliability]. Princeton's tracker of AI agents, which this site reads, scores each agent's accuracy and reliability from nought to one, and across the agents it has tested accuracy has risen by [fact:hal_accuracy_trend] and reliability by [fact:hal_reliability_trend], where a point is a hundredth of that range. AI 2027's story also has agents stumbling in their first years, so the gap settles nothing yet.

[plate:reliability]

The fastest clock settles nothing either. The length of the software tasks AI can finish doubles every [fact:horizon_doubling], at least as fast as AI 2027 assumed, but neither side doubts that single skills race ahead. Whole jobs separate them. On the Remote Labor Index, which scores models on real paid freelance projects completed end to end, the best model manages [fact:rli_record]. The compounding story, as written, needs most of those projects done by the end of 2027; the slowest-step story expects whole projects to trail single skills for years.

[plate:frontier]

### Folio II · Who checks the work?

## Whether checking AI's work becomes a business turns on who must answer for it

Markets run on knowing whom you are dealing with. Gillian Hadfield, who designs legal and regulatory systems for AI, and Andrew Koh, who studies how to design markets, point out that AI agents have none of the identity, registration or records that markets rely on, so each agent must be tied to a person or firm that answers for it, or be given legal standing and assets a court could seize [cite:hadfield_koh]. This site carries their argument one step further: if someone must answer for an agent's work, someone may be paid to check it. In February 2026 Gartner, which advises companies on what to buy, published a guide to the firms that sell platforms for testing and watching AI systems, and since January 2026 insurers have had standard wording to write generative AI, the kind that writes and draws, out of their policies. The rival view is that the labs, the companies that build the most capable models, and the big cloud companies, which rent out computing, give checking away with their own platforms, and no reading yet tells the two apart.

Soren Larson, a co-founder of a company that routes businesses' requests to AI models, who writes about how money moves between the labs and the apps built on them, thinks whoever stands between a lab and its customers gets squeezed. An app reselling a lab's model pays at least the lab's own price per token, the fragment of a word in which the use of a model is sold, and can charge little more than going to the lab directly would cost, so its margin, what is left of revenue after the cost of what was sold, shrinks towards whatever its own additions are worth [cite:larson_squeeze]. His argument rests on one observation: "To my knowledge labs do not offer special wholesale pricing" [cite:larson_squeeze]. Nobody publishes app margins, so it cannot be tested yet.

Platforms face the mirror image. Peyman Shahidi, John Horton and their colleagues, economists who study online markets, argue that agents could slash the cost of searching and bargaining, and expect platforms to set rules for how outside agents may use them, much as websites tell search engines' crawlers, the programs that read the web for them, what they may read [cite:shahidi_etal]. Byrne Hobart and Nikhil Davar, who write The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology, read Amazon's blocking of Meta's shopping assistant in September 2026 the other way: platforms gain enough from controlling their customers' dealings with AI to keep outside agents out [cite:hobart_inference]. Amazon had already gone to court in November 2025 to keep Perplexity's shopping agent off its site, while Etsy and Walmart agreed to let shoppers buy through OpenAI's chatbot. This site's hand-kept ledger for the past year puts fences at [fact:fences_ledger] and openings at [fact:openings_ledger], but it does not yet sweep both sides under one rule, so it tests nothing yet.

### Folio III · Is adoption slow, or just hard to see?

## Adoption at the pace of past technologies fits both stories, so the argument turns on what the statistics miss

Narayanan and Kapoor's larger argument is that AI is a normal technology, whose big effects on the economy will come over decades, at the pace at which people and institutions change how they work [cite:normal_tech]. The Census Bureau's survey of American businesses fits their account so far: [fact:firms_using_ai] of firms say they used AI in the past two weeks to make what they sell, in line with the pace of past technologies rather than faster. History suggests the harder part comes after arrival. Diego Comin and Martí Mestieri, economists who study how technologies spread between countries, found that new technologies now reach poor countries almost as fast as rich ones, but that poor countries use them far less intensively, and that this gap in depth explains most of the difference in incomes [cite:comin_mestieri].

[plate:adoption]

Diane Coyle and John Lourenze Poquiz, economists at Cambridge who study how the economy is measured, reply that most use of AI is free and its gains come as better work and saved time, which the official statistics do not price, so measured output can lag, or even fall, while people are better off [cite:coyle_poquiz]. Paying consumer subscribers number only [fact:paid_share] of ChatGPT's weekly users. That fits both stories: people may not pay because the tool is not yet worth much, or because its value never passes through a till.

The clearest early sign may be in hiring. Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen, economists at Stanford who study AI and work through payroll records, found that workers in their early twenties in the jobs most exposed to AI have fallen behind their less exposed peers, mostly because firms hire fewer of them [cite:canaries]. They describe the pattern without claiming to have proved its cause, so the comparison carries the weight. With each group's employment set at a hundred in November 2022, the young now stand at [fact:junior_gap] against workers over fifty in the most exposed fifth of jobs, and at [fact:junior_gap_control] in the least exposed. If the gap opened everywhere, something other than AI would be the likelier culprit.

### Folio IV · Does work reorganise fast enough to show up in output?

## Two economists have bet against an explosion, and tonight's reading is one both sides expected

The cleanest test here is a bet. Benjamin Moll, an economist at the London School of Economics who studies whole economies, and Alex Imas, who studies behaviour and AI at Chicago Booth, are bullish on what AI will be able to do and still think growth of more than ten percent a year in the next decade or so extremely unlikely, since it would need several unlikely things at once, from fast automation across the economy to AI that automates research itself [cite:moll_imas]. In August 2026 they and five others took the other side of a bet from four people who bet that in some quarter before 2034 American real output per person, output after inflation divided by the population, will stand [test:bet_fast_side] or more above the highest level it had reached a year or more before [cite:bet_fast_side]. Among the four is William MacAskill, a moral philosopher at Forethought, a research group on advanced AI, who with Fin Moorhouse has argued that AI could compress a century of technological progress into a decade [cite:macaskill_moorhouse]. Tonight output per person stands [fact:gdp_pc_over_peak] above that level [cite:moll_imas_bet].

Charles Jones and Christopher Tonetti, economists at Stanford who study long-run growth, supply the slow side's arithmetic: work is a chain of tasks that substitute poorly for one another, so if AI follows the pattern of past automation, growth rises only slowly, to less than three percent a year even by 2075, while in their fastest calibration, in which machines improve everywhere at once, it passes seven percent by 2030 [cite:jones_tonetti]. Nor would a fast path necessarily show early. Anton Korinek, Peter McCrory and colleagues, Charles Jones among them, economists who model growth under advanced AI and several of whom work for or advise Anthropic, turned assumptions about AI into paths for the economy, which they present as scenarios rather than forecasts, and found that "Across scenarios, almost all of the divergence comes after 2027" [cite:korinek_etal].

Even where AI works, the first thing it changes may not be hours. In 1930 John Maynard Keynes, whose work founded modern macroeconomics, suggested that within a century his grandchildren might share out the little work left in a week of about fifteen hours [cite:keynes]. Betsey Stevenson, a labour economist at Michigan, expects the opposite order: the washing machine raised the standard of a clean house long before it shortened the hours spent on housework, and AI, she argues, will first raise how much people are expected to do [cite:stevenson].

The bet settles it by 2034 at the latest. Output per person grew by [fact:gdp_pc_yoy] in the latest year, close to Jones and Tonetti's slow path [cite:jones_tonetti], though a reading like that fits the fastest of Korinek and colleagues' scenarios until about 2027 as well.

### Folio V · Who keeps the money?

## Whether the labs keep their margins turns on how fast open models catch up

Carlota Perez, an economist who studies technological revolutions and the financial bubbles that come with them, found the same sequence in each of the five great surges of technology since 1771: a frenzy of investment that runs ahead of the uses, a crash, then a golden age in which the technology is put to work [cite:perez]. The builders of the infrastructure rarely keep the value, note Arvind Narayanan and Akash Kapur, a senior fellow at New America who studies how AI is governed, with cloud computing and the leading chip foundry, a factory that makes chips for others, as partial exceptions. Selling access to the frontier models, the most capable ones, looks like a commodity business, where buyers choose on price alone, so the labs' likeliest escape, they argue, is to move up the stack, into products and deployments built into their customers' work, where switching is costly [cite:nk_up_the_stack].

Hobart puts the commodity case plainly: once some labs give away open models, whose inner workings anyone may download and run, the price of the cheapest models is set by the chips and power that run them, and a model has more pricing power where it is the best tool for a particular job [cite:hobart_round_trip] [cite:hobart_pacing]. Larson answers with a result from Simon Board and Marek Pycia, economists who study how sellers set prices over time. A seller who could cut its price is usually forced to, by buyers who wait for discounts; but if buyers can walk away to another option instead, "the seller charges a constant price in every period equal to the monopoly price" [cite:board_pycia], the price a seller with no rivals would set. For AI, the open model is the other option: the lab's price holds and the volume leaves, as long as open models improve too slowly for buyers to wait for them [cite:larson_durability].

The readings so far fit both. Open models carry [fact:open_share] of the tokens routed to the busiest models on OpenRouter, a marketplace that passes developers' requests to many models, and trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag]. At list prices, among the open models that can be matched with a closed one as capable, the labs' own cheaper models even undercut them, costing a median [fact:open_premium] as much, though that is a single reading so far. Meanwhile the chip makers take [fact:chips_gp_share] of the gross profit, revenue less the direct cost of what was sold, shared by chips, cloud and the labs, and the biggest cloud and platform companies spend [fact:capex_to_revenue] as much a year on buildings and equipment as AI earns in revenue. David Cahn, an investor at Sequoia Capital, has raised his estimate of the revenue AI must earn to pay that spending back every year since 2023, though he now sees in AI's help with writing code a clearer way to earn it [cite:cahn_2026].

[plate:stack]

The price of the best model will settle it. If it falls towards the open models' as the gap closes, the commodity view wins; if it holds while the volume leaves, Larson's does.

### Where they agree

## A handful of points recur across these writers, and not only on one side

Selling access to a model, token by token, is a thin business; someone has to answer for what an AI agent does before it can be trusted with work that matters; checking AI's work becomes a costly task of its own; and people use AI well before firms reorganise around it. Where someone here dissents, the dissent is listed with the point.

### The futures still open

## Crossing progress with rules shows which futures tonight's readings still allow

How fast capability improves and how the rules on deploying AI settle will decide which future arrives. So far the rules have got lighter: the American president ordered moves against state AI laws in December 2025 [cite:eo_14365], Colorado replaced its AI Act with a narrower law on automated decisions in May 2026 [cite:colorado_sb26_189], and the European Union put off its rules for high-risk AI until the end of 2027 and beyond [cite:eu_2026_1744]. Narayanan and Kapoor had argued years earlier that licensing who may build models would not work [cite:nk_licensing].

The grid crosses the two and fills a cell only where a named writer argues it; a cell stays open while none of its signposts is failing its test, and every open cell is marked, never just one. What would close cells, and change the outlook: whole paid projects done end to end, the best model's price holding or falling as open models close in, independent firms winning the checking, platforms fencing or opening, and output per person breaking away before 2030.

[plate:scenarios]

### Every claim, tested nightly

## A claim earns its place by naming what would prove it wrong

Every claim on this page, each writer's and this site's own, is listed with its test, tonight's reading and the outcome that would prove it wrong. The tests run every night, so a claim that stops holding says so here before anyone rewrites a sentence.

[plate:board]

folios.kicker: Can AI do whole jobs, reliably?
Is adoption slow, or just hard to see?
Does work reorganise fast enough to show up in output?

positions.case: AI coding agents improved faster in 2026 than even these forecasters expected, and they brought their dates forward again [cite:ai_futures_update], though their own check finds events running a little slower than the story [cite:ai_futures_q25].
positions.kill_shot: Whole jobs staying far out of reach while single skills race ahead, which is the pattern a pace set by the slowest step predicts.
positions.mechanism: Each model helps write the code and run the experiments that build the next one, so progress feeds on itself.
positions.title: AI speeds up its own research, and the gains compound

positions.case: The best models finish ever longer software tasks, yet only a small part of the whole paid projects they are set.
positions.kill_shot: A huge speed-up on a single step that makes overall progress explode, which Jones names as the evidence that would refute him.
positions.mechanism: Superhuman speed on some steps leaves the others, still slow, setting the pace of the whole.
positions.title: Research moves at the pace of its slowest step

positions.case: The same agents that solve more tasks each year still give different answers when the same task is run again.
positions.kill_shot: Reliability rising as fast as accuracy.
positions.mechanism: A firm hands work to an agent only when it behaves the same way each time, and that has improved far more slowly than accuracy.
positions.title: Getting a task right is not getting it right every time

positions.case: Firms that sell the labs expert-written practice work have grown fast; Surge AI was reported in 2025 to have passed [fact:surge_revenue] in yearly revenue.
positions.kill_shot: The next model taking the missing steps by itself, so that paying to teach them buys nothing a lab would not soon have anyway.
positions.mechanism: If progress moves at the pace of the steps AI cannot take [cite:jones_b], the scarce thing is the next step a model can be taught, and that can be paid for, with practice tasks and graders sold to the labs, and with the work of fitting a model to the steps a firm's own jobs need.
positions.title: The missing steps can be bought

positions.case: AI already helps build AI, yet progress has looked steady rather than explosive.
positions.kill_shot: Each new model's gains on AI research arriving faster than the last's, with nothing lost along the way.
positions.mechanism: The research AI can automate is narrow, and people and budgets still set the pace.
positions.title: Self-improvement leaks

positions.case: What scaling laws measure is how well a model guesses the next word, not whether it can do a job.
positions.kill_shot: Size alone producing abilities that no change in method explains.
positions.mechanism: Scaling laws promise better guessing of the next word, not any particular new ability, and good data is running out.
positions.title: Bigger models alone will not get there

positions.case: Gartner, which advises companies on what to buy, has published a guide to the platforms that sell such checking, and insurers can now write AI's mistakes out of their standard policies.
positions.kill_shot: Checking staying a free feature of the labs' and cloud companies' own platforms.
positions.mechanism: Someone has to verify what an agent did and answer when it is wrong, and buyers will pay for that. Hadfield and Koh argue for the registration and the accountability; this site carries it to a market.
positions.title: Checking AI's work becomes a business of its own

positions.case: A lab that wants firms to trust its agents has every reason to supply the checks itself.
positions.kill_shot: Independent checkers winning large contracts that the platforms' free tools could have filled.
positions.mechanism: The labs and cloud companies already test and watch their own models, and can give that away to keep their customers.
positions.title: Checking stays a free feature of the big platforms

positions.case: As far as Larson knows, labs sell to apps at the prices they list for everyone, so an app's margin is only what its own additions are worth.
positions.kill_shot: Labs selling to apps below their public prices.
positions.mechanism: An app cannot pay less than the lab charges for its model, nor charge much more than going to the lab directly would cost its customers.
positions.title: Apps that resell the labs' models get squeezed

positions.case: Firms pay for tools that fit their work, not for raw access to a model.
positions.kill_shot: Apps' margins falling as their customers' use rises.
positions.mechanism: Data, workflow and the customer relationship are hard to copy, even when the model underneath is not.
positions.title: Apps keep their margin through what they build around the model

positions.case: Amazon went to court to keep an AI browser's shopping agent off its site, and later blocked Meta's shopping assistant.
positions.kill_shot: Platforms opening to outside agents through shared rules and protocols.
positions.mechanism: A platform that owns the customer loses that tie if someone else's agent does the shopping, so it pays to keep outside agents out and run its own.
positions.title: Big platforms fence out agents that are not their own

positions.case: Etsy and Walmart have agreed to let shoppers buy through OpenAI's chatbot, Etsy on an open standard for agents to pay.
positions.kill_shot: Platforms blocking or suing outside agents more often than they sign them up.
positions.mechanism: Platforms will set rules for how outside agents may use them, much as websites tell search engines' crawlers what they may read, and a platform that lets agents in keeps the sale when a chatbot finds the product.
positions.title: Platforms set terms for outside agents and let them in

positions.case: Buyers pay for tasks a model can be trained to improve on, and those are scarce.
positions.kill_shot: Models learning such work from practice they set and grade themselves.
positions.mechanism: Teaching models long work whose results are hard to check needs practice tasks and graders that people must build.
positions.title: Checked practice work is the next shortage

positions.case: A task whose answer a machine can check can be practised endlessly, at the cost of the computing alone.
positions.kill_shot: Progress stalling in work a machine cannot grade until people build the graders.
positions.mechanism: Where a computer can check the answer, as in mathematics and code, a model can practise without people writing the answers, and the checking can spread from there.
positions.title: Models make their own practice

positions.case: The share of American firms using AI has risen at the pace of past technologies, not faster.
positions.kill_shot: Measured adoption jumping to the pace this site calls fast.
positions.mechanism: Firms have to rebuild processes, train people and carry liability before a tool pays, and that takes years.
positions.title: Adoption is slow because the frictions are real

positions.case: Only a small share of the people using the biggest AI assistant pay for it.
positions.kill_shot: The paid share of use rising to where the statistics would see most of it.
positions.mechanism: Most use of AI is free and its gains come as quality and saved time, which the official statistics do not price.
positions.title: Adoption is not slow; it is hard to see

positions.case: In the jobs most exposed to AI, young workers have fallen behind older ones; in the least exposed jobs they have not.
positions.kill_shot: Young workers falling behind in the least exposed jobs as well, which would point to a cause other than AI.
positions.mechanism: A firm that can do a junior's work with AI hires fewer juniors before it lets anyone go.
positions.title: Junior hiring shows it first

positions.case: The study itself describes a pattern rather than proving its cause; the gap survives controls for firms' exposure to interest rates but narrows once workers' education is taken into account.
positions.kill_shot: The gap staying confined to the most exposed jobs as those other causes fade.
positions.mechanism: Interest rates, the hiring boom after the pandemic and its unwinding hit young workers first, whatever AI does.
positions.title: Young workers' troubles have causes other than AI

positions.case: Selling a house is easier to delegate than buying one, and the first traction is in job search, property and matching.
positions.kill_shot: Agents spreading first in markets where people rarely hire human agents.
positions.mechanism: Handing a task to an agent is easiest where people already hire agents and can say simply what they want.
positions.title: Agents arrive first where wants are simple and agents already work

positions.case: Larson points to the largest retail platforms shutting out independent shopping agents in favour of their own.
positions.kill_shot: Independent agents dealing on firms' behalf at scale in open markets.
positions.mechanism: When everyone has the same models, what a firm knows about its own needs is its edge, and asking the market for help gives it away.
positions.title: Asking reveals what you want, so firms keep work inside

positions.case: Code that comes with tests is handed to AI before contracts that come with none.
positions.kill_shot: Work that is hard to check being handed over as fast as work that is easy to check.
positions.mechanism: A task is handed over when checking the result costs less than doing it. Hadfield and Koh argue about accountability; this site carries the argument to the order of adoption.
positions.title: What goes first is set by the cost of checking, not the cost of doing

positions.case: Moll and Imas expect AI's abilities to keep leaping and still think growth of four to five percent a year, which would itself be historic, is the reasonable expectation [cite:moll_imas].
positions.kill_shot: A quarter before 2034 in which output per person clears the bet's line above its level of a year or more before.
positions.mechanism: An explosion would need fast automation across the economy, spending that follows it, demand that absorbs the output, no costly accidents and AI that automates research, all at once; and work is a chain of tasks that substitute poorly for one another, so AI that follows the pattern of past automation raises growth only slowly [cite:jones_tonetti].
positions.title: Growth rises, but does not explode

positions.case: MacAskill and three others have put money on growth exploding before 2034 [cite:bet_fast_side], and in Korinek and colleagues' model a fast path looks like the others until about 2027 [cite:korinek_etal], so slow readings now do not count against it.
positions.kill_shot: No qualifying quarter before 2034, on the bet's own terms.
positions.mechanism: Once AI's thinking rivals the whole of humanity's, it keeps growing far faster than the number of people, research speeds up enormously and industry follows, so output can break away within a decade.
positions.title: AI compresses a century of progress into a decade

positions.case: Appliances in the middle of the twentieth century raised standards of cleanliness long before they shortened the hours spent on housework.
positions.kill_shot: Paid hours in the most exposed work falling before output rises.
positions.mechanism: A tool that makes work easier first raises what people are expected to produce, as washing machines raised the standard of a clean house.
positions.title: Work gets more intense before it frees time

positions.case: If AI multiplies what an hour of work produces, the same needs can be met with fewer hours.
positions.kill_shot: Hours in the most exposed work rising as AI spreads.
positions.mechanism: As output per hour rises, people take part of the gain as leisure and share out the work that remains. Keynes argued it of machines in general in 1930; this site carries it to AI.
positions.title: Machines buy people time

positions.case: Richer households spend a larger share of their money on care, teaching and hospitality.
positions.kill_shot: Pay in that work falling behind pay elsewhere as AI spreads.
positions.mechanism: As machines make other things cheap, spending moves to work where the person is part of what is bought.
positions.title: Work built on people dealing with people gains

positions.case: In Restrepo's model labour's share of income heads towards nothing once computing can do any work, even as total wages rise.
positions.kill_shot: Wages rising smoothly with output as AI spreads.
positions.mechanism: Where better algorithms set the pace, wages jump and fall as tasks are automated [cite:restrepo]; where AI is sold with market power, Athey and Scott Morton add, workers pay again when its price rises [cite:athey_scott_morton].
positions.title: Wages follow a jagged path, and the displaced can lose again

positions.case: Early evidence, by the authors' account, fits bigger firms and less local autonomy.
positions.kill_shot: Firms getting smaller and more decentralised as they adopt AI.
positions.mechanism: AI captures the local knowledge that used to justify leaving decisions to people on the spot.
positions.title: Decisions move to the centre

positions.case: The knowledge Hayek meant is the kind nobody writes down, so no model trained on what is written holds it.
positions.kill_shot: Firms that move decisions to the centre with AI outperforming those that leave them local.
positions.mechanism: What matters for most decisions is knowledge of particular times and places, which changes too fast to be sent to the centre. Hayek argued it about central planning; this site carries it to AI.
positions.title: Knowledge on the spot keeps decisions there

positions.case: Cloudflare counts AI companies' crawlers, the programs that read websites for them, taking far more pages than they send visitors back, on news sites as elsewhere [cite:cloudflare_crawl], though it warns the count may be overstated where an app does not say where its visitors came from [cite:cloudflare_ratio].
positions.kill_shot: Visits to publishers from search and AI answers rising.
positions.mechanism: Sites that produce information are paid by visits, and AI that answers directly sends fewer of them.
positions.title: Answers replace visits, and the web that trained AI loses its income

positions.case: Cloudflare, which stands between many websites and their visitors, bought an AI data marketplace to build a system in which AI developers pay for the content they train on [cite:cloudflare_human_native].
positions.kill_shot: Publishers' income falling even where they charge AI companies.
positions.mechanism: As answers replace visits, publishers charge the AI companies directly, by licence or by the page.
positions.title: AI companies pay for what they read

positions.case: Open models trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag], months rather than years.
positions.kill_shot: The labs' prices holding while open models close the gap.
positions.mechanism: Where some labs give their models away, the cheapest price is set by the chips and power that run them, and a lab has more pricing power where its model is the best tool for the job.
positions.title: Tokens become a commodity

positions.case: Near-frontier open models sell for a small fraction of the best model's price without, as Larson reads it, denting the best model's sales.
positions.kill_shot: Open models improving fast enough that buyers wait for them rather than pay, the condition Larson himself states.
positions.mechanism: Buyers who will not pay a lab's price leave for an open model rather than wait for a discount, so the lab keeps its price and serves fewer of them; Simon Board and Marek Pycia proved the result for any seller whose buyers can walk away [cite:board_pycia].
positions.title: The price holds, and the volume leaves

positions.case: Cloud computing escaped the same trap by becoming software, and the leading chip foundry by being almost alone.
positions.kill_shot: The labs' revenue staying mostly in selling access to their models.
positions.mechanism: Selling access to a model is a commodity business, so labs move into products and into deployments built into their customers' work, where switching is costly; Athey and Scott Morton add that a supplier with market power can raise its price later [cite:athey_scott_morton].
positions.title: Labs escape by moving up the stack, and lock their customers in

positions.case: Hobart reads the reports that Meta may use other firms' models for some of its answers this way.
positions.kill_shot: The owners of the best models taking users from the biggest platforms.
positions.mechanism: A platform with the most users gains most by serving good-enough models to all of them and selling better ones on top, whoever built them.
positions.title: The biggest platforms win with models that are good enough

positions.case: In Larson's own simulation a central router beat each firm's own choices on a standard test of AI agents, most of all on new kinds of problems.
positions.kill_shot: Firms choosing models as well on their own as a router does.
positions.mechanism: A neutral router sees many firms' problems, so it learns which model to use faster than any one firm, and pricing by outcome belongs with it.
positions.title: Routers gain power

positions.case: This is the line in this site's essay on the migrating bottleneck, and Larson's argument contradicts it.
positions.kill_shot: Routers' share of traffic and their margins rising as models converge.
positions.mechanism: The better a router works, the more easily buyers move to the cheapest model that is good enough, the harder sellers compete on price, and the less anyone needs a router.
positions.title: A router works itself out of a job

positions.case: The chip makers take [fact:chips_gp_share] of the gross profit shared by chips, cloud and the labs.
positions.kill_shot: The chip makers' share falling while chips stay scarce.
positions.mechanism: When every input is needed at once, the one hardest to get sets the pace and its owner takes the profit, until the industry builds its way out.
positions.title: Whoever holds the scarcest input collects

positions.case: The biggest cloud and platform companies spend [fact:capex_to_revenue] as much a year on buildings and equipment as AI earns in revenue.
positions.kill_shot: AI's revenue growing into the spending before the chips it bought are out of date.
positions.mechanism: The spending on data centres has to be paid back by revenue that has not arrived yet, and the chips it buys lose value fast, so if the revenue comes late the investors take the loss.
positions.title: The money runs out before the revenue arrives

positions.case: Cahn wrote in December 2025 that a few such delays had already been reported publicly.
positions.kill_shot: The new capacity coming online on schedule, with the price of computing falling as it arrives, the other outcome Cahn names.
positions.mechanism: Demand for computing runs into a supply chain that has not grown as fast, from the few firms that make the most advanced chips and the machines that make them to generators, cooling and skilled builders, so data centres are finished late while use keeps rising.
positions.title: The build-out runs late while use keeps rising

positions.case: Sundheim points to the labs' coding tools and the paid access to their models as businesses customers stick with.
positions.kill_shot: Customers switching between models freely on price, or more than a handful of labs staying at the frontier.
positions.mechanism: Customers could switch between models as easily as between clouds but mostly do not, and staying at the frontier costs too much capital for more than a handful of labs.
positions.title: The labs are durable businesses with high margins

positions.case: Across American business after the Second World War, innovators kept about two cents of each dollar of value they created [cite:nordhaus].
positions.kill_shot: AI firms' profits growing as fast as the value their users get.
positions.mechanism: Competition and imitation pass most of an innovation's value to the people who use it, through lower prices; the innovators keep a sliver. Nordhaus measured it across American business after the Second World War; this site carries it to AI.
positions.title: Consumers keep most of the value

anchors.text: The American president ordered moves against state AI laws and called for a light national standard.
Standard exclusions for harm caused by generative AI became available for insurers to attach to general liability policies.
Colorado replaced its AI Act with a narrower law on automated decisions, which applies from January 2027.
The European Union's changes to its AI Act came into force, putting off its rules for high-risk AI until December 2027 and August 2028.

cells.says: Models stop getting much better at whole jobs, and the gains come from spreading what already works.
The spending outruns the revenue it needs, the builders slow down before the uses arrive, and the losses fall on their investors.
Capability keeps improving, firms adopt it at the pace of past technologies, and growth rises without exploding.
Courts and insurers settle who pays for AI's mistakes, and adoption speeds up where the rules are clear.
Agents and the firms behind them must register before they deal; licensing who may build the models, Narayanan and Kapoor argue, would not work.
Each model speeds up the research behind the next, output breaks away, and wages settle at the cost of the computing that could replace a person.
In the story's slower ending, oversight slows the race until the systems can be checked, and governments spend far more on safety than they do now.

rules.label: Courts and insurers price the risk

sources.field: forecasters of AI progress at the AI Futures Project; Kokotajlo worked on governance at OpenAI
sources.finding: A dated story in which AI labs use each model to speed up the research that builds the next, ending with AI that outdoes people at almost everything by the end of 2027. The authors say 2027 was their single most likely year, and their middle estimates were later.
sources.who: Daniel Kokotajlo, Eli Lifland, Thomas Larsen and Romeo Dean, with Scott Alexander

sources.field: the same forecasters, revising their own dates
sources.finding: After pushing their dates for fully automated coding later at the end of 2025, the authors brought them forward again, because AI coding agents had improved faster than they expected.
sources.who: Eli Lifland, Daniel Kokotajlo and colleagues
sources.work: Q1 2026 Timelines Update

sources.field: the same forecasters, checking their story against events
sources.finding: Checked against what has happened, the story is roughly on track but running a little slower, at around three quarters of its pace.
sources.who: Eli Lifland, Daniel Kokotajlo and colleagues
sources.work: Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update: Uplift and Revenue

sources.field: an economist at Northwestern who studies where growth and scientific progress come from
sources.finding: Research needs every step done, so an AI that is superhumanly good at some steps lifts overall progress only a little while other steps stay slow; what counts is the share of steps it can take over. He adds that checking the work becomes a task of its own, and that AI able to check itself would spare costly human checking.
sources.quote: bottlenecks severely mute the effect of extremely productive AI
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: Artificial Intelligence in Research and Development

sources.field: Princeton researchers who test AI agents
sources.finding: Large gains in how often agents solve tasks brought only small gains in how dependably they do it; agents still answer differently on repeat runs and break when instructions are reworded, and though they have become better at telling when they will fail, they are not much more consistent.
sources.who: Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, Arvind Narayanan and colleagues
sources.work: Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability

sources.field: Hadfield designs legal and regulatory systems for AI; Koh studies how to design markets and incentives
sources.finding: AI agents lack the identity and registration systems markets rely on, so either each agent is tied to a registered person or firm that answers for it, or agents get legal standing with assets a court could seize.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: An Economy of AI Agents

sources.field: a co-founder of an AI gateway company who writes about how money moves between AI labs and the apps built on them
sources.finding: Apps that resell a lab's models are squeezed between the lab's price per token and what customers would pay to go to the lab directly, so as use grows their profit shrinks towards nothing unless their revenue stops tracking tokens.
sources.quote: To my knowledge labs do not offer special wholesale pricing
sources.work: The Smart Squeeze

sources.field: economists and computer scientists who study online markets; Fradkin works for Amazon and Horton advises Anthropic
sources.finding: Agents could slash the cost of searching, bargaining and contracting; they will be taken up first where people already hire human agents and can state simply what they want, and platforms will set rules for how outside agents may use them, much as websites tell search engines' crawlers what they may read, though some already block them.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.who: Peyman Shahidi, Gili Rusak, Benjamin Manning, Andrey Fradkin and John Horton
sources.work: The Coasean Singularity?

sources.field: writers of The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology; Hobart discloses that he holds shares in Amazon
sources.finding: Amazon blocked Meta's shopping assistant from its site; the authors read it as a sign that companies gain enough from controlling their customers' dealings with AI to pay for the computing themselves rather than let another firm's agent in.
sources.work: Forward Deployed (the section Fighting for Inference)

sources.field: computer scientists at Princeton who study what AI can and cannot do
sources.finding: AI's large effects on the economy will arrive over decades, at the pace at which people and institutions adopt it, as with electricity and the internet. Unclear liability deters firms from adopting a technology, and clear rules speed it up.
sources.work: AI as Normal Technology

sources.field: economists who study how technologies spread between countries
sources.finding: Across two centuries, new technologies have come to reach poor countries almost as fast as rich ones, but poor countries use them far less intensively, and that gap in the depth of use explains most of the divergence in incomes.
sources.work: If Technology Has Arrived Everywhere, Why Has Income Diverged?

sources.field: economists at Cambridge who study how the economy is measured
sources.finding: Official statistics will capture AI's contribution poorly and late, because most use is free and its gains in quality and saved time are not priced, so measured output can lag or even fall while people are better off.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.who: Diane Coyle and John Lourenze Poquiz
sources.work: Making AI Count

sources.field: economists at Stanford's Digital Economy Lab who study AI and work through payroll records
sources.finding: Employment of workers in their early twenties in the jobs most exposed to AI has fallen behind that of their less exposed peers, mostly through less hiring, while experienced workers show no such gap. The authors describe the pattern; they do not claim to have proved its cause.
sources.who: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen
sources.work: Canaries in the Coal Mine?

sources.field: Moll is a macroeconomist at the London School of Economics; Imas studies behavioural economics and AI at Chicago Booth
sources.finding: Growth of more than ten percent a year in the next decade or so is extremely unlikely even if AI's abilities leap, because it would need several unlikely things at once, from fast automation across the economy to AI that automates research itself; four to five percent a year would already be massive. They are bullish on AI's abilities and have bet against an explosion.
sources.work: Will AI soon lead to double-digit growth?

sources.field: the four who took the fast side of the growth bet; MacAskill is a moral philosopher at Forethought, a research group that studies how to prepare for advanced AI
sources.finding: They bet that in some quarter before 2034 American real output per person will stand fifteen percent or more above the highest level it had reached a year or more before.
sources.short: the fast side of the growth bet
sources.who: William MacAskill, Samuel Albanie, Tom Cohen and Jan Kulveit
sources.work: Growth bet terms

sources.field: researchers at Forethought, a research group that studies how to prepare for advanced AI; MacAskill, a moral philosopher, taught at Oxford until 2024
sources.finding: Once AI's thinking rivals the whole of humanity's, it will keep growing far faster than the number of people, so a century of technological progress could be compressed into a decade, followed by an explosion in industry.
sources.work: Preparing for the Intelligence Explosion

sources.field: the terms of a public bet agreed in August 2026
sources.finding: Seven people, Moll and Imas among them, bet against four others that in no quarter before 2034 will American real output per person stand fifteen percent or more above the highest level it had reached a year or more before; the fast side wins as soon as one quarter does, and nothing reopens it.
sources.who: Benjamin Moll, Alex Imas and five others
sources.work: Growth bet terms

sources.field: economists at Stanford who study long-run growth
sources.finding: Past automation raised productivity through ever better machines, but work is a chain of tasks that substitute poorly for one another, so weak links tame the explosion; if AI follows the pattern of past automation, growth rises only slowly, and only if machines improve everywhere at once does it break away within a few years.
sources.work: Past Automation and Future A.I.: How Weak Links Tame the Growth Explosion

sources.field: economists who model growth under advanced AI; several work for or advise Anthropic
sources.finding: A model that turns assumptions about AI into paths for the economy to 2030, from barely changed to growing far faster than today; the authors present them as scenarios, not predictions.
sources.quote: Across scenarios, almost all of the divergence comes after 2027.
sources.who: Anton Korinek, Charles Jones, Peter McCrory and colleagues
sources.work: Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI

sources.field: the economist whose work founded modern macroeconomics
sources.finding: Within a century, technical progress would raise living standards so far that the economic problem would be largely solved, and he suggested people might share out the little work left in three-hour shifts, a fifteen-hour week.
sources.venue: an essay, reprinted in his Essays in Persuasion
sources.work: Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren

sources.field: a labour economist at the University of Michigan
sources.finding: The danger is not too little output but gains that reach most people late and unevenly; as with household appliances, AI will first raise how hard and how well people work before it frees their time.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: What Is There to Fear in a Post-AGI World?

sources.field: an economist who studies technological revolutions and the financial bubbles that come with them
sources.finding: Each of the great surges of technology since 1771 has gone the same way, a frenzy of investment that runs ahead of the technology's uses, a crash and a remaking of the rules, then a golden age in which the technology is put to work; the full benefits come only after decades of turbulent adjustment.
sources.work: Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital

sources.field: Narayanan is a Princeton computer scientist; Kapur, a senior fellow at New America, studies how AI is governed
sources.finding: Selling access to frontier models looks like a commodity business, so the labs' likeliest path to lasting profit is moving up the stack into products and deployments built into their customers' work, which escapes the trap at the price of lock-in. The builders of past infrastructure rarely kept the value, with cloud computing and the leading chip foundry as partial exceptions.
sources.work: Up the Stack: How AI's Escape From the Commodity Trap Risks Enterprise Lock-in

sources.field: the writer of The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology, after work in digital advertising and investment research
sources.finding: Once some AI labs give their models away as open weights, the price of the cheapest models is set by the chips and power that run them; he reads a chip-equipment maker's investment in an open-model lab as keeping AI labs many and chip demand high.
sources.work: The Autistic Half-Century (the section Round-Tripping)

sources.field: the writer of The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology, after work in digital advertising and investment research
sources.finding: Models have more pricing power where they are the best tool for a particular job; labs that agree to slow their best releases are also agreeing not to widen their lead over open models.
sources.work: The Economics and Politics of Pacing the Frontier

sources.field: economic theorists who study bargaining and how sellers set prices over time
sources.finding: A seller free to cut its price over time is normally forced down by buyers who wait for discounts; when buyers can take another option instead, the only equilibrium is the seller charging the monopoly price every period.
sources.quote: the seller charges a constant price in every period equal to the monopoly price
sources.work: Outside Options and the Failure of the Coase Conjecture

sources.field: a co-founder of an AI gateway company who writes about how money moves between AI labs and the apps built on them
sources.finding: Applying Board and Pycia, buyers who will not pay a lab's price leave for an open model rather than wait for a discount, so a lab can keep a high price while its market shrinks as open models close the gap; the price holds only while open models improve too slowly for buyers to wait for them.
sources.work: Durability of Frontier AI

sources.field: an investor at Sequoia Capital who backs AI and infrastructure companies
sources.finding: His running estimate of the revenue needed to pay back each year's spending has grown every year since he first posed the question in 2023, though he now sees in AI's help with writing code a clearer way to earn it back.
sources.work: AI's $1.5T Question

sources.field: an executive order
sources.finding: Calls for a light national standard for AI, to be proposed to Congress, and moves against state AI laws through a federal task force to challenge them in court, a list of burdensome state laws and conditions on federal grants; it names Colorado's law as the kind it means.
sources.who: The President of the United States
sources.work: Executive Order 14365: Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence

sources.field: a state law
sources.finding: Repeals the state's AI Act and replaces it with a narrower law on automated decisions about jobs, housing, lending and the like, from January 2027.
sources.work: SB26-189, Automated Decision-Making Technology

sources.field: a regulation amending the EU's AI Act
sources.finding: Simplifies the AI Act and puts off its rules for high-risk AI, to December 2027 for most systems and August 2028 for AI built into regulated products.
sources.who: The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union
sources.work: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI

sources.field: computer scientists at Princeton who study what AI can and cannot do
sources.finding: Licensing who may build powerful AI models would need ever more intrusive surveillance as training gets cheaper, and would hand the industry to a few firms.
sources.work: Licensing is neither feasible nor effective for addressing AI risks

sources.field: a machine-learning researcher who builds and writes about open language models
sources.finding: AI already helps build AI, but the loop leaks, because the research it can automate is narrow, adding agents gives less and less, and budgets and people still set the pace; so progress looks steady rather than explosive.
sources.work: Lossy self-improvement

sources.field: computer scientists at Princeton who study what AI can and cannot do
sources.finding: Scale has brought new abilities before, but scaling laws predict only how well a model guesses the next word, not which abilities appear, and good data is running out, so making models bigger is unlikely on its own to produce general intelligence.
sources.work: AI scaling myths

sources.field: an economist at Stanford who studies long-run growth and the economics of AI's risks
sources.finding: By the reasoning about the value of a life that the United States used during Covid, spending at least one percent of output a year to cut the risk of an AI catastrophe is justified in most scenarios, far more than is spent now.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: How Much Should We Spend to Reduce AI's Existential Risk?

sources.field: an investor and writer who works in the market for training data
sources.finding: The scarce input is realistic, well-checked training data, meaning practice tasks, grading rubrics and quality checks for long work whose results are hard to verify.
sources.work: An AI Bubble is a human data problem

sources.field: a co-founder of an AI gateway company who writes about how money moves between AI labs and the apps built on them
sources.finding: Cheap agents make dealing with outsiders costlier, not cheaper, because asking a market for anything reveals what you want to your competitors; so firms keep work inside, platforms shut out outside agents, and firms split into the very large and the very small.
sources.work: Against The Coasean Singularity

sources.field: an economist at Chicago Booth who studies behaviour and AI
sources.finding: As AI makes mass-produced things cheap and people richer, spending and jobs shift towards relational work, where the person doing it is part of the value, such as care, teaching and hospitality.
sources.work: What will be scarce?

sources.field: a Yale economist who studies how technology shapes work and pay, and a member of Anthropic's economic advisory council
sources.finding: Once AI can turn computing power into any kind of work, wages settle at what the computing to replace a person costs and labour's share of income heads towards nothing even as total wages rise; the path is jagged when better algorithms, not more computing, set the pace.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: We Won't Be Missed

sources.field: economists who study competition and technology; both served as chief economist of the US antitrust division
sources.finding: When AI is sold by firms with market power, the workers it displaces can lose twice, once when cheap AI cuts their pay and again when its price later rises.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.who: Susan Athey and Fiona Scott Morton
sources.work: Artificial Intelligence, Competition, and Welfare

sources.field: Brynjolfsson directs Stanford's Digital Economy Lab; Hitzig studies AI's effects on society, now at the Anthropic Institute and at OpenAI when the chapter was written
sources.finding: AI can capture the local, unwritten knowledge that once argued for leaving decisions to people on the spot, so decisions centralise, with bigger firms, more concentrated industries and less room for local managers.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: AI's Use of Knowledge in Society

sources.field: an economist who studied how prices carry what people know
sources.finding: The knowledge an economy runs on is scattered among the people on the spot and never exists whole in any one place, so decisions about particular circumstances have to be left to them, with prices telling them what they need to know.
sources.work: The Use of Knowledge in Society

sources.field: Stiglitz won the Nobel prize for work on markets where one side knows more than the other; Ventura-Bolet is a doctoral fellow at Columbia
sources.finding: News and other information is paid for by visits, and AI that answers directly diverts them, so without rules on credit and accountability less true information gets made.
sources.venue: The Economics of Transformative AI (National Bureau of Economic Research)
sources.work: The Impact of AI and Digital Platforms on the Information Ecosystem

sources.field: the writer of The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology; he discloses that he holds shares in Meta and Alphabet
sources.finding: For the biggest social network, the ideal is not owning the best model but having the best distribution for models that are good enough, then selling its users up to better ones, built in-house or not.
sources.work: Rumor Markets (the section AI and Complements)

sources.field: a co-founder of an AI gateway company who writes about how money moves between AI labs and the apps built on them
sources.finding: Paying for AI by the outcome belongs at a neutral router that sees many firms' problems, because a central router learns which model to use faster than any one firm while new kinds of problems keep arriving.
sources.work: Router Power

sources.field: a Yale economist who studies growth and productivity, and who won the Nobel prize for bringing climate change into long-run economics
sources.finding: Across American business from the end of the Second World War to the turn of the century, innovators kept only a tiny share of the value their innovations created, about two cents in the dollar; most of it went to consumers through lower prices.
sources.venue: National Bureau of Economic Research working paper
sources.work: Schumpeterian Profits in the American Economy: Theory and Measurement

sources.field: an investor at Sequoia Capital who backs AI and infrastructure companies
sources.finding: The revenue AI must earn to pay back a year's spending on data centres runs far ahead of what it earns; the chips lose value fast and computing rented by the hour has little pricing power, so if the revenue comes late the investors take the loss, while founders building on cheap computing gain.
sources.work: AI's $600B Question

sources.field: a writer for the Independent Insurance Agents and Brokers of America, reporting on the standard policy wordings that ISO, a unit of Verisk, drafts for insurers
sources.finding: New optional endorsements with a January 2026 edition date let insurers exclude harm arising from generative AI from general liability policies; each insurer chooses whether to attach them.
sources.work: Verisk to Roll Out New General Liability Exclusions for Generative AI Exposures

sources.field: an investor at Sequoia Capital who backs AI and infrastructure companies
sources.finding: Expects the coming year to bring delays, with data centres finished late while use keeps rising; the cloud companies storing new chips instead of installing them would be the sign the delays had begun.
sources.work: AI in 2026: A Tale of Two AIs

sources.field: the head of global equity research at Goldman Sachs, and a former analyst of chip makers
sources.finding: Spending of about a trillion dollars on AI's infrastructure has to be paid back by solving hard, valuable problems, and he doubted AI was built to do that, or that its costs would fall as those of past technologies did; he still expected the spending to go on for a while.
sources.work: Gen AI: too much spend, too little benefit?

sources.field: the founder of an investment firm that holds stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic
sources.finding: The old worry that selling access to AI models would become a commodity business no longer matters; customers could switch between models but mostly do not, margins are high, and only a handful of labs will matter because staying at the frontier costs too much capital. The open question is whether the returns on the spending arrive in time.
sources.venue: Invest Like the Best, a podcast, on YouTube
sources.work: Inside Dan Sundheim's Bets on Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX

sources.field: economists who study technology, firms and productivity
sources.finding: A general-purpose technology needs large investments in new processes, skills and ways of doing business that the national accounts mostly miss, so measured productivity looks weak in the technology's early years and strong later, when the investments pay off.
sources.who: Erik Brynjolfsson, Daniel Rock and Chad Syverson
sources.work: The Productivity J-Curve: How Intangibles Complement General Purpose Technologies

sources.field: a company that stands between many websites and their visitors, reporting on its own traffic
sources.finding: AI companies' crawlers, the programs that read websites for them, take far more pages than they send visitors back, including on news and publication sites, where Anthropic's crawler took thousands of pages for each visitor it sent.
sources.work: A deeper look at AI crawlers: breaking down traffic by purpose and industry

sources.field: a company that stands between many websites and their visitors, reporting on its own traffic
sources.finding: Its count of pages crawled for each visitor sent back may overstate the gap where an app, such as Anthropic's, does not say where its visitors came from, by an amount it cannot tell.
sources.work: The crawl before the fall of referrals: understanding AI's impact on content providers

sources.field: a news report
sources.finding: Cloudflare bought Human Native, a British start-up that handles payments from AI developers to the creators whose work they train on, to build a system in which AI developers pay for the content they use.
sources.work: Cloudflare acquires AI data marketplace Human Native
